1. Using the same model outlined in [recitation 2](../recitations/recitation-2.qmd) and [recitation 3](../recitations/recitation-3.qmd), solve two versions of the model with $\rho = 0.95$ and $\rho=0.1$. In both versions, hold the *unconditional* variance of $\varepsilon$ fixed at its value in the recitations, $\sigma^2_{\varepsilon} = 0.1^2/(1-0.9^2)$, by setting $\sigma_{\zeta} = \sigma_{\varepsilon}\sqrt{1-\rho^2}$. Keep all other parameters the same as in the recitations. Explain in one or two sentences why we hold the unconditional variance fixed rather than $\sigma_{\zeta}$. Then compare welfare in the two economies using the consumption equivalent averaged over the stationary distribution, as in recitation 2:
$$ 1+\omega = \left[\frac{\sum_{y}\pi^*_{0.1}(y)V_{0.1}(0,y)}{\sum_{y}\pi^*_{0.95}(y)V_{0.95}(0,y)}\right]^{1/(1-\sigma)}$$
where $V_{\rho}$ and $\pi^*_{\rho}$ are the value function and the stationary distribution of $\Pi$ in the economy with persistence $\rho$. Interpret your answer.

2. Given agents live for $T$ periods ($t=0,\dots,T-1$), note that for a guaranteed consumption level $\bar{c}$, we have:
$$ \mathcal{V}(\bar{c}) = \sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\beta^{t}u(\bar{c}) = \frac{1-\beta^{T}}{1-\beta}u(\bar{c}).$$
Given this, show that:
$$ \bar{c}(y) = \left[(1-\sigma)\frac{1-\beta}{1-\beta^{T}}V(0,y)\right]^{1/(1-\sigma)} $$
is the certainty equivalent: the consumption level that, if delivered with certainty in every period, would achieve the same value as $V(0,y)$.

3. Assume that the government now levies a 10\% proportional income tax that it then redistributes as a lump sum. Thus, net income for an agent is
$$ \tilde{y} = 0.9 \times y + 0.1\times\mathbb{E}[y] $$
where $\mathbb{E}[y] = \sum_{y}\pi^*(y)y$ and $\pi^*$ is the stationary distribution of the transition matrix $\Pi$. Write code to solve the model with this system of taxes and transfers. Show that this net income function respects the aggregate resource constraint (this should take only one line to prove).

4. Define 
$$W^{r} = \sum_{y}\pi^*(y)V^{r}(0,y) = \mathbb{E}[V^{r}(0,y)]$$
to be utilitarian welfare under regime $r\in\{A,B\}$ where regime $A$ is the laissez-faire economy and regime $B$ is the economy with taxes and transfers. Let $\bar{C}^{r} = \sum_{y}\pi^*(y)\bar{c}^{r}(y)$ be the average certainty equivalent in regime $r$. For both models (each value of $\rho$), calculate the decomposition of the consumption equivalent welfare gain from [Lecture 2](../lectures/2-Insurance_vs_Redistribution.qmd) and [recitation 3](../recitations/recitation-3.qmd), $1+\omega = (1+\omega_{I})(1+\omega_{R})$, where:
$$\begin{aligned}
1+\omega &= \left[\frac{W^{B}}{W^{A}}\right]^{1/(1-\sigma)} &\text{(total gain)}\\
1+\omega_{I} &= \left[\frac{\mathcal{V}(\bar{C}^{B})}{\mathcal{V}(\bar{C}^{A})}\right]^{1/(1-\sigma)} = \frac{\bar{C}^{B}}{\bar{C}^{A}} &\text{(gain from insurance)}\\
1+\omega_{R} &= \left[\frac{W^{B}/\mathcal{V}(\bar{C}^{B})}{W^{A}/\mathcal{V}(\bar{C}^{A})}\right]^{1/(1-\sigma)} &\text{(gain from redistribution)}
\end{aligned}
$$

5. Comment on the difference in this decomposition for $\rho=0.95$ vs $\rho=0.1$. Can you give some intuition for the difference? (**extra credit** )
